cues.text: In 1430, a woman in Monaco purchased a monstrance from a secondhand dealer.
She was unaware—or perhaps only later realized—that it still contained a large consecrated Host, almost certainly because the vessel itself had been stolen from a church.
Unfamiliar with Catholic teaching on the Real Presence, the woman decided to remove the Host from the monstrance using a knife.

As she did, living Blood is said to have begun flowing from it, drying almost immediately and leaving behind, imprinted on the Host itself, an image of Christ seated on a throne, flanked by instruments of his Passion.
From a Frightened Woman to a Pope
Unsettled by what she had done, the woman brought the Host to a local canon named Anelon, who kept it in his own care.
Word of the event spread quickly enough to reach Pope Eugene IV, who arranged for the Host to be given to Duke Philip of Burgundy.
The duke in turn donated it to the city of Dijon, where it was enshrined in the Basilica of St. Michael the Archangel.
Three and a Half Centuries, Then Fire

The Host remained intact and venerated at Dijon for more than 350 years — a span of continuous devotion unusually long even among Eucharistic relics of this era — until the French Revolution reached the city.

On February 9, 1794, revolutionary authorities requisitioned the basilica to consecrate it as a temple to the Cult of Reason, and the miraculous Host, along with much else the Revolution regarded as superstition, was destroyed.
Though the relic itself did not survive, its memory did.
Numerous period documents and works of art record the event, including a stained-glass window in Dijon Cathedral.
It still depicts the central scene of a startled woman, a knife, and an image that appeared where none had been painted.

The Dijon account stands as a reminder that even relics venerated across many generations are not guaranteed permanence — that devotion sometimes has to be content with memory alone, once the object itself has been lost.
